stimulus: Many people assume that deserts are nearly lifeless, but the surface of desert soil is often covered by a thin crust of cyanobacteria, lichens, and mosses. This biological soil crust binds loose sand together, slows erosion by wind and water, and adds nitrogen to soil that would otherwise be too poor to support many plants. When the crust is crushed by vehicles or livestock, it can take decades to recover.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Deserts contain more species of plants than most people assume.
Biological soil crusts perform important functions in deserts and are slow to recover once damaged.
Vehicles cause more damage to desert soils than livestock do.
Cyanobacteria are the most important organisms in desert ecosystems.
rationale: The text describes what the crust does (binds sand, slows erosion, adds nitrogen) and ends by noting it takes decades to recover. B captures both parts. A overstates plant diversity, C compares two causes the text never ranks, and D singles out one organism the text treats as part of a group.

stimulus:
The following text is from a story. Wen has just started working in her aunt's bakery.

Wen had imagined that the bakery would smell of sugar all day, but by six in the morning her arms ached from lifting sacks of flour, and her apron was stiff with dough. Her aunt moved between the ovens without hurrying, never wasting a step. Watching her, Wen realized that what she had taken for calm was actually years of practice.
stem: Based on the text, what does Wen come to understand about her aunt?
choices: Her aunt would prefer to work alone.
Her aunt is less skilled than Wen had expected.
Her aunt dislikes the smell of the bakery.
Her aunt's apparent ease is the result of long experience.
rationale: The last sentence says Wen realized the aunt's calm "was actually years of practice." Nothing in the text supports the other choices.

stimulus: Agronomist Lucía Ferrer hypothesizes that planting strips of wildflowers along the edges of tomato fields increases tomato yields because the flowers attract native bees, which are more effective pollinators of tomatoes than honeybees are.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ferrer's hypothesis?
choices: Fields with wildflower strips had more visits from native bees to tomato flowers and higher tomato yields than fields without strips.
Tomato fields with wildflower strips had more honeybee visits than fields without them, but yields were the same.
Native bees were more abundant near fields with wildflower strips, but tomato yields in those fields did not differ from yields in fields without strips.
Wildflower strips required more water than tomato plants did.
rationale: The hypothesis links three things: wildflower strips → more native bees on tomatoes → higher yields. Only A shows all three together. B and C show no yield difference, which weakens the hypothesis, and D is irrelevant to pollination.

stimulus:
Average weekly attendance at Harbor Street Library programs

| Program | 2021 | 2022 | 2023 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Coding club | 14 | 22 | 31 |
| Book club | 25 | 24 | 26 |
| Chess club | 18 | 12 | 9 |

A librarian at Harbor Street Library tracked average weekly attendance at three programs. She concluded that interest in the coding club grew steadily over the period, while attendance at the chess club declined.
stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the librarian's conclusion?
choices: Average weekly attendance at the coding club rose from 14 in 2021 to 31 in 2023, while attendance at the chess club fell from 18 to 9.
The book club had the highest average weekly attendance in 2021 and in 2023.
The chess club had higher average weekly attendance than the coding club did in 2021.
Average weekly attendance at the book club changed by only a few people each year.
rationale: The conclusion is about two trends: coding club up, chess club down. A cites both. B and D are about the book club, and C compares the two clubs in a single year rather than showing a change over time.

stimulus: Glaciologists measuring a glacier in Alaska found that its surface was lowering by about a meter per year, yet its front edge had barely moved in a decade. The researchers noted that the glacier's front rests on a thick pile of rock and sediment that the glacier itself pushed into place over centuries. This finding suggests that ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the glacier is gaining ice faster than it is losing it.
the sediment pile may be holding the glacier's front in place even as the glacier thins.
glaciers that rest on sediment always thin more slowly than other glaciers.
measurements of glacier surfaces are less reliable than measurements of glacier fronts.
rationale: The puzzle is a thinning glacier whose front doesn't retreat; the sediment pile at the front is offered as the explanation. A contradicts the thinning, C overgeneralizes with "always," and D is not suggested anywhere.

stimulus: In many songbird species, young males learn their songs by copying adult tutors. Researchers raised zebra finches without any adult tutor; these birds still developed songs, but the songs were atypical. When the untutored birds later tutored a new generation, and that generation in turn tutored another, the songs moved closer to the typical zebra finch song with each generation. This result implies that ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: zebra finches cannot learn songs from birds of their own generation.
untutored zebra finches are unable to serve as effective tutors.
some features of typical zebra finch song may emerge from learning tendencies in the birds themselves rather than being passed down intact.
the songs of tutored zebra finches become less typical over successive generations.
rationale: Starting from atypical songs, the population drifted back toward the typical song without ever hearing it, so the birds themselves must bias learning toward those features. B is contradicted (their pupils did learn), D reverses the finding, and A is never tested.

stimulus:
Percentage of borrowers returning overdue books within one week

| Group | Returned within 1 week |
|---|---|
| No message | 22% |
| Reminder message only | 31% |
| Fine waiver only | 38% |
| Reminder message + fine waiver | 47% |

Economists studied whether a reminder text message and a waiver of late fines affected how quickly people returned overdue library books. They concluded that the reminder and the fine waiver each increased returns on their own, and that combining them was more effective than using either one alone.
stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the economists' conclusion?
choices: Compared with 22% for no message, 31% of borrowers returned books after a reminder alone, 38% after a fine waiver alone, and 47% after both.
The fine waiver alone was more effective than the reminder message alone.
More than one-fifth of borrowers returned their books within one week even without a message.
The combination of the reminder and the fine waiver produced the highest return rate of any group.
rationale: The conclusion has two parts: each intervention helps on its own (both beat 22%), and the combination beats each alone (47% vs. 31% and 38%). Only A supports both. D is tempting but shows only the second part.

stimulus: Community gardens in several cities have begun lending out tools the same way libraries lend books. Members can borrow a shovel, pruning shears, or a wheelbarrow for a week at a time. Organizers say the programs save members money and reduce the number of rarely used tools that end up stored in garages.
stem: According to the text, what is one benefit organizers say tool-lending programs provide?
choices: They teach members how to repair tools.
They increase the number of community gardens.
They help members save money.
They allow members to keep tools permanently.
rationale: The last sentence states that organizers say the programs "save members money." D contradicts the one-week loan period, and A and B are not mentioned.

stimulus:
The following text is from a poem. The speaker addresses an old house.

You kept the rain out for a hundred years
and never asked a thing of us but paint.
Now I walk your rooms and hear the stairs
complain beneath me, low, without restraint.
I patch the sills; I tell you you are fine.
We both know better. Still, I paint the trim.
stem: Which quotation from the poem most effectively illustrates the claim that the speaker continues to care for the house despite recognizing that it is declining?
choices: "You kept the rain out for a hundred years"
"and never asked a thing of us but paint."
"Now I walk your rooms and hear the stairs"
"We both know better. Still, I paint the trim."
rationale: The claim needs both halves: awareness of decline and continued care. "We both know better" admits the decline, and "Still, I paint the trim" shows the care continuing. The other lines show only the house's past or the speaker's presence.

stimulus: Although the new bridge design looked ______ on paper, engineers worried that it had never been tested in the strong crosswinds common at the site.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: promising
dangerous
invisible
crowded
rationale: "Although" sets up a contrast with the engineers' worry, so the design must have looked good on paper. "Promising" fits; "dangerous" would agree with the worry rather than contrast with it.

stimulus: The chef's approach to seasoning is notably ______: she adds salt in tiny amounts, tastes the dish, and adds more only if necessary.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: careless
generous
cautious
random
rationale: The text after the colon describes small, deliberate additions checked by tasting, which is a cautious approach. The other words contradict that description.

stimulus: In her study of nineteenth-century letters, historian Amira Haddad argues that the writers' frequent apologies for their "poor penmanship" should not be taken at face value. Such apologies were a social convention, a way of appearing modest, rather than a ______ assessment of their handwriting.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: flattering
public
lengthy
sincere
rationale: Haddad says the apologies were a convention "rather than" a genuine judgment, and "should not be taken at face value." "Sincere" is the opposite of a mere convention. "Flattering" is illogical for an apology about one's own handwriting.

stimulus: For decades, astronomers assumed that the rings of Saturn formed along with the planet, about 4.5 billion years ago. Data from the Cassini spacecraft complicated that view: the rings are remarkably free of the dark dust that should have accumulated on them over billions of years. Some researchers now argue that the rings may be only a few hundred million years old, though others contend that processes not yet understood could keep old rings clean.
stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It presents a long-held assumption, describes evidence that challenges it, and notes a disagreement about how to interpret that evidence.
It describes a spacecraft mission and then lists that mission's most important discoveries.
It explains why a new theory has been widely rejected by astronomers.
It compares the rings of Saturn with the rings of other planets.
rationale: Sentence 1 gives the old assumption, sentence 2 the Cassini evidence against it, and sentence 3 the two competing interpretations. The text neither lists discoveries (B), reports a rejection (C), nor mentions other planets (D).

stimulus: Many city planners favor wide streets because they move traffic efficiently. However, studies of pedestrian behavior show that people are less likely to walk along streets that feel wide and exposed. Narrower streets with trees and ground-floor shops, by contrast, tend to draw foot traffic, which in turn supports local businesses.
stem: Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence in the overall structure of the text?
choices: It provides an example that supports the claim in the first sentence.
It introduces a drawback of the approach described in the first sentence.
It summarizes the findings described in the third sentence.
It explains why city planners have abandoned wide streets.
rationale: "However" signals a turn: sentence 1 gives the case for wide streets, and sentence 2 gives a cost (people avoid walking on them). The text never says planners have abandoned wide streets (D).

stimulus:
Text 1
Some linguists argue that the rapid spread of text messaging has weakened young people's formal writing, pointing to abbreviations and missing punctuation in school essays. In their view, habits formed on phones inevitably carry over into other kinds of writing.

Text 2
Linguist Dara Okafor studied thousands of essays and text messages written by the same students. She found that abbreviations common in the students' texts almost never appeared in their essays, and that students who texted most frequently were no worse at formal punctuation than those who texted least. Okafor concludes that students readily switch between styles of writing depending on context.
stem: Based on the texts, how would Okafor (Text 2) most likely respond to the view of the linguists in Text 1?
choices: She would agree that texting harms formal writing but argue that the effect is smaller than they claim.
She would argue that students who text frequently tend to write longer essays.
She would agree with their conclusion but criticize them for focusing on abbreviations rather than punctuation.
She would argue that their assumption that texting habits carry over into formal writing is not supported by evidence from students' actual writing.
rationale: Okafor's data show texting abbreviations don't appear in essays and heavy texters punctuate just as well, which directly contradicts the Text 1 claim that habits "inevitably carry over." A and C have her agreeing, which her findings don't support; B is about essay length, which she never measured.

stimulus: The biologist's account of octopus problem-solving is careful not to overstate its case: where the evidence is thin, she offers her interpretations as ______ rather than as settled conclusions.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: provisional
exhaustive
dismissive
conventional
rationale: The blank contrasts with "settled conclusions" and matches not overstating thin evidence. "Provisional" means tentative and open to revision. "Exhaustive" would imply the opposite of thin evidence.

stimulus:
The following text is from a novel. Imogen, a young violinist, is preparing for an audition.

She had played the concerto so many times that her fingers found the notes before she thought of them. That was the trouble. In the practice room the music ran on without her, smooth and correct and entirely empty, and she stood listening to it the way one listens to a radio in another apartment.
stem: Which choice best describes the main purpose of the text?
choices: To suggest that Imogen has not practiced the concerto enough
To describe the physical setting in which Imogen practices
To convey Imogen's sense that her technically accurate playing lacks personal engagement
To explain why Imogen chose to perform a concerto
rationale: The playing is "smooth and correct" but "entirely empty," and she hears it like a distant radio, which is detached from her own music. A reverses the problem (she has practiced too much), and B and D are not the focus.

stimulus: Sea otters eat large numbers of sea urchins, which feed on kelp. ______ where sea otters are present, kelp forests tend to be healthier and more extensive.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: However,
For example,
As a result,
Similarly,
rationale: Otters eating urchins that eat kelp causes healthier kelp forests, so the second sentence is a consequence of the first. "As a result" signals that cause and effect.

stimulus: The earliest bicycles had no pedals; riders pushed themselves along with their feet. ______ pedals were attached directly to the front wheel, which led some manufacturers to build enormous front wheels to increase speed.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: Therefore,
Later,
For instance,
Nevertheless,
rationale: The text moves through stages of bicycle design in time order, so a time transition is needed. "Later" marks the next stage. The second sentence is not a consequence, example, or concession.

stimulus: Many early photographs show subjects with stern, unsmiling expressions. It is often assumed that this was because long exposure times made holding a smile difficult. ______ some historians argue that social conventions played a larger role: a broad smile was considered foolish or improper in a formal portrait.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: However,
Consequently,
Likewise,
In other words,
rationale: The final sentence offers an explanation that challenges the common assumption in the previous sentence, so a contrast transition is needed.

stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

- Rice terraces are built as a series of flat steps cut into hillsides.
- Each terrace holds water, which flows downward from one level to the next.
- The terraces reduce soil erosion on steep slopes.
- Terraced farming is practiced in parts of Asia, South America, and Africa.
stem: The student wants to explain how rice terraces help farmers on steep land. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Terraced farming is practiced in parts of Asia, South America, and Africa.
By cutting hillsides into flat steps that hold water and reduce soil erosion, rice terraces allow farmers to grow crops on steep slopes.
In rice terraces, water flows downward from one level to the next.
Rice terraces are a series of flat steps found on several continents.
rationale: The goal is how terraces help on steep land. B explains the mechanism (flat steps, water, reduced erosion) and the benefit. The others state facts without connecting them to farming steep slopes.

stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

- Researchers compared two methods of restoring a degraded grassland.
- Method 1: planting seeds of native grasses.
- Method 2: planting the same seeds and adding a small amount of soil taken from a healthy grassland.
- After three years, plots restored with Method 2 had 40% more native plant cover than plots restored with Method 1.
- The added soil contained fungi and microbes that help plants absorb nutrients.
stem: The student wants to emphasize a difference between the results of the two methods. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Researchers compared planting native grass seeds alone with planting seeds and adding soil from a healthy grassland.
The soil added in Method 2 contained fungi and microbes that help plants absorb nutrients.
After three years, plots that received healthy grassland soil along with seeds had 40% more native plant cover than plots that received seeds alone.
Both methods involved planting seeds of native grasses in a degraded grassland.
rationale: The goal is a difference in results. Only C reports outcomes for both methods and the gap between them. A describes the methods, not results; B explains a possible cause; D stresses a similarity.

stimulus: Early maps of the Pacific often showed islands that did not exist, the result of sailors misjudging their positions. Some of these "phantom islands" stayed on charts for a remarkably long time. ______ Sandy Island, supposedly located between Australia and New Caledonia, appeared on some maps until 2012, when a research vessel sailed through the spot and found only open ocean.
stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: Consequently,
Nevertheless,
By contrast,
In one notable case,
rationale: Sandy Island is an example of a phantom island that stayed on charts for a long time, so the transition should introduce an illustration. It is not a result, a concession, or a contrast.

stimulus: The museum's newest exhibit features more than two hundred ______ many of them collected by a single amateur naturalist in the 1800s.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: fossils,
fossils;
fossils.
fossils and
rationale: "Many of them collected…" is not an independent clause, so it can't follow a semicolon or period. A comma correctly attaches this descriptive phrase to the main clause. "And" would create an ungrammatical sentence.

stimulus: The collection of handwritten recipes, which spans four generations of the Morales family, ______ now displayed at the town's historical society.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: are
were
is
have been
rationale: The subject is the singular "collection," not "recipes," and "now" calls for present tense. "Is" is singular and present.

stimulus: Each of the robotic rovers sent to Mars has carried instruments designed for ______ specific mission.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: their
its
it's
they're
rationale: The antecedent is the singular "each," so a singular possessive pronoun is needed: "its." "It's" means "it is."

stimulus: Marine biologist Keiko Sato studies how coral reefs recover after ______ her work combines underwater surveys with satellite imagery.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: storms,
storms
storms, which
storms;
rationale: Both sides of the blank are independent clauses. A semicolon can join them; a comma alone creates a comma splice, no punctuation creates a run-on, and "which" produces a sentence that doesn't make sense.

stimulus: In 1869, the first transcontinental railroad in the United States was completed. Before then, a journey from the East Coast to California ______ several months by wagon or by ship.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: takes
has taken
had taken
will take
rationale: The journey happened before another past event (1869), so the past perfect "had taken" is correct. The other choices are present, present perfect, or future.

stimulus: The novel's narrator, a retired lighthouse keeper named Elias ______ tells the story entirely in letters to his estranged daughter.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: Brand;
Brand—
Brand,
Brand
rationale: The appositive "a retired lighthouse keeper named Elias Brand" opens with a comma, so it must close with a comma. A dash would not match the opening comma, and a semicolon would split the subject from its verb.

stimulus: In her essay, the critic singles out one quality that sets the director's films apart from those of her ______ a refusal to explain her characters' motives.
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: peers:
peers,
peers;
peers
rationale: The sentence builds to "one quality" and then names it. A colon introduces that explanation after a complete clause. A comma would make the phrase seem to describe "peers"; a semicolon needs an independent clause after it.

stimulus: Having spent six months cataloging the specimens in the museum's basement, ______
stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: the collection was finally ready for the public to see.
the public was finally able to see the collection.
the opening of the collection to the public finally occurred.
the curators finally opened the collection to the public.
rationale: The opening phrase describes whoever spent six months cataloging, so that person must come right after the comma. Only "the curators" could have done the cataloging; the other choices create dangling modifiers.
